In the last lecture, you covered different ways that someone might set up and exploit a covert channel. In the last lab, you set up a storage covert channel using the file permissions of an FTP server.

In this lab, you will build a **timing covert channel**. You will set up a server that transmits an ordinary text message one character at a time, but encodes a *secret* message in the pauses between each successive character.

As an example: a delay of 25 ms between characters could represent a `0`, while a delay of 100 ms represents a `1`. The overt message is perfectly readable by anyone; only a receiver who knows the encoding scheme can recover the hidden message.

In order to transfer a longer covert message, you will need a longer overt message — each overt character carries exactly one covert bit. Using the values above, transmitting a single covert character (7 or 8 bits) requires transmitting at least 8 overt characters. This is not unreasonable: covert channels are typically **low bandwidth**, trading efficiency for secrecy.

To signal the end of the covert message, the sender appends the string `"EOF"` (encoded in binary like any other text) to the covert bitstream. The receiver stops decoding once it detects this sentinel.

:::{.callout-note}
This lab uses **Rust**. You only need the standard toolchain — no external crates. Create a project with `cargo new covert_server` (and another for the client), then edit `src/main.rs`. Build and run with `cargo run`.
:::

# Setting Up the Server

## A Basic Chat Server {#sec-basicserver}

Let's start with a basic TCP server using Rust's standard `std::net` module. This first version acts as an **echo server** — it accepts connections, reads any message the client sends, and echoes it back. This gives you a working baseline to test before adding covert channel logic.

```rust
/*
*  std::io gives us buffered reading and the Write trait, std::net gives
*  us the TCP types, and std::thread lets us handle each client on its
*  own thread.
*/
use std::io::{BufRead, BufReader, Write};
use std::net::{TcpListener, TcpStream};
use std::thread;

// Constants make the server easy to tweak without hunting through code.
const ADDRESS: &str = "0.0.0.0"; // all IPv4 interfaces.
                                 // Use "127.0.0.1" to restrict to local connections only.
const PORT: &str = "1337";       // choose an unprivileged port (> 1024) not in common use

fn main() {
    // Start listening for TCP connections on the specified address and port.
    let listener = match TcpListener::bind(format!("{ADDRESS}:{PORT}")) {
        Ok(l) => l,
        // If the server can't start (e.g. port already in use), exit with an error.
        Err(e) => {
            eprintln!("Error starting server: {e}");
            std::process::exit(1);
        }
    };

    println!("Server listening on {ADDRESS}:{PORT}");

    // Accept and handle connections indefinitely. `incoming()` yields one
    // result per inbound connection.
    for stream in listener.incoming() {
        match stream {
            Ok(conn) => {
                println!("New client connected!");

                // Handle each connection on its own thread so the server
                // can serve multiple clients concurrently. `move` hands
                // ownership of the connection to the thread.
                thread::spawn(move || handle_connection(conn));
            }
            Err(e) => {
                // A bad incoming connection shouldn't crash the server —
                // log it and move on to the next one.
                eprintln!("Error accepting connection: {e}");
                continue;
            }
        }
    }
}

// handle_connection reads messages from the client and echoes them back.
fn handle_connection(stream: TcpStream) {
    // A TcpStream is both readable and writable, but wrapping it in a
    // BufReader takes ownership, so we clone the handle first: one copy
    // to read through, one to write through. Both point at the same socket.
    let mut writer = stream.try_clone().expect("failed to clone stream");
    let mut reader = BufReader::new(stream);
    let mut line = String::new();

    loop {
        line.clear();
        // read_line reads until it finds the delimiter '\n'.
        match reader.read_line(&mut line) {
            // 0 bytes read means the client has disconnected.
            Ok(0) => {
                println!("Client disconnected.");
                return;
            }
            Ok(_) => {
                print!("Message received: {line}");

                // Echo the message back to the client.
                if writer.write_all(format!("You said: {line}").as_bytes()).is_err() {
                    return;
                }
            }
            Err(e) => {
                eprintln!("Error reading from client: {e}");
                return;
            }
        }
    }
}
```

:::{.callout-tip}
This is a great place to pause and test your server before adding timing logic.

You don't need a custom client yet — use one of these built-in terminal tools:

**telnet** (plain text, unencrypted — do not use for sensitive data):
```sh
telnet localhost 1337
```

**netcat** (general-purpose network utility):
```sh
nc localhost 1337
```

Press `Ctrl+C` or type `exit` to disconnect. You can also share your server's IP address with a classmate and have them connect from their machine:

```sh
telnet ip.ad.re.ss 1337   # or
nc    ip.ad.re.ss 1337
```
:::

## Sending an Overt Message One Character at a Time

The echo server above is just a starting point. To build our covert channel we need to make two key changes:

1. **Stop reading from the client** — our server only needs to *send*, not receive.
2. **Send the overt message one character at a time**, with a deliberate delay after each character. That delay is where the covert message lives.

Bring the sleep and duration types into scope:

```rust
use std::thread::sleep;
use std::time::Duration;
```

Add timing constants alongside your existing ones:

```rust
const ADDRESS: &str = "0.0.0.0";
const PORT: &str = "1337";
const ZERO: u64 = 25;   // milliseconds — delay to signal a 0 bit
const ONE: u64 = 100;   // milliseconds — delay to signal a 1 bit
```

The ratio between `ZERO` and `ONE` (here 4×) should be large enough that clock jitter on the receiving side does not cause a misread. A good rule of thumb: the receiver classifies any delay above the midpoint `(ZERO + ONE) / 2 = 62.5 ms` as a `1`.

:::{.callout-important}
**Disable Nagle's algorithm.** By default, TCP batches together small outgoing writes (Nagle's algorithm) to cut down on packet overhead. That batching would smear our carefully timed per-character delays together and destroy the covert signal. Go happens to disable Nagle automatically on TCP connections; **Rust does not**, so we call `stream.set_nodelay(true)` ourselves before sending. This pushes each character out in its own packet, the moment we write it.
:::

Now replace `handle_connection` with a new function `send_message` that sends the overt message character by character:

```rust
fn send_message(message: &str, mut stream: TcpStream) {
    // Send each character immediately instead of letting TCP buffer them.
    let _ = stream.set_nodelay(true);

    for (i, ch) in message.chars().enumerate() {
        if stream.write_all(ch.to_string().as_bytes()).is_err() {
            eprintln!("Error writing to client");
            return;
        }

        /*
        * For now, alternate between one and zero delays based on
        * position — just to verify the timing mechanism works before
        * we wire in the actual covert bitstream.
        */
        if i % 2 == 0 {
            sleep(Duration::from_millis(ONE));
        } else {
            sleep(Duration::from_millis(ZERO));
        }
    }

    println!("Overt message sent. Closing connection.");
    // The stream is dropped here, which closes the connection.
}
```

Update `main` to use the new function:

```rust
// Inside the `for stream in listener.incoming()` loop, in the Ok(conn) arm:
let message = String::from("This is a perfectly ordinary message that will be sent one character at a time.");

// thread::spawn(move || handle_connection(conn));   <- replace this
thread::spawn(move || send_message(&message, conn)); // <- with this
```

## Encoding the Covert Message

We now have a server that sends a message with timing delays. The final step is to replace the alternating dummy delays with delays driven by the actual covert bitstream.

The helper function `get_covert` converts a string to its binary representation — one 8-bit sequence per character, concatenated into a single string. Note that the `"EOF"` sentinel is appended to the covert message so the receiver knows when to stop decoding. No extra imports are needed; `String` and `format!` are in the standard prelude.

```rust
fn get_covert() -> String {
    let covert = String::from("secret") + "EOF";
    let mut result = String::new();

    for b in covert.bytes() {
        // {:08b} formats the byte as an 8-bit binary string, left-padded
        // with zeros. For standard ASCII text, iterating the bytes is
        // exactly the character's ASCII value in binary.
        result.push_str(&format!("{b:08b}"));
    }
    result
}
```

As an example: if `covert == "ABC"`, then `get_covert()` returns `"010000010100001001000011"`.

Now update `send_message` to look up the covert bit for each character position and choose the appropriate delay:

```rust
fn send_message(message: &str, mut stream: TcpStream) {
    let _ = stream.set_nodelay(true);

    let covert = get_covert();
    let covert = covert.as_bytes(); // index into the '0'/'1' characters as bytes

    for (i, ch) in message.chars().enumerate() {
        if stream.write_all(ch.to_string().as_bytes()).is_err() {
            eprintln!("Error writing to client");
            return;
        }

        // Use modulo so the covert message repeats if the overt
        // message is longer than the covert bitstream.
        if covert[i % covert.len()] == b'1' {
            sleep(Duration::from_millis(ONE));
        } else {
            sleep(Duration::from_millis(ZERO));
        }
    }

    println!("Overt message sent. Closing connection.");
}
```

:::{.callout-tip}
Make sure your overt message is **at least as long as** your covert bitstream. Each covert character requires 8 overt characters. The word `"secret"` plus the `"EOF"` sentinel is 9 characters × 8 bits = 72 bits, so the overt message must be at least 72 characters long.
:::

# Setting Up the Client

:::{.callout-tip}
Timing covert channels depend on accurate sleep and clock measurements. These have historically been less reliable on Windows and inside virtual machines. This is our first attempt using Rust — so you will be our guinea pigs. Rust's `Instant` is a monotonic, high-resolution clock and `thread::sleep` is fine for our millisecond-scale delays, but the OS scheduler and TCP buffering still add jitter. If your measurements are inconsistent, try widening the gap between `ZERO` and `ONE`, confirm `set_nodelay(true)` is enabled on the server, or run on a native Linux machine.
:::

## A Basic Chat Client

Let's start with a basic client that can connect to the echo server from @sec-basicserver, send messages, and display the server's responses. This gives you a working foundation before adding timing measurement logic.

```rust
use std::io::{self, BufRead, BufReader, Write};
use std::net::TcpStream;

fn main() {
    let stream = match TcpStream::connect("localhost:1337") {
        Ok(s) => s,
        Err(e) => {
            eprintln!("Error connecting: {e}");
            std::process::exit(1);
        }
    };

    println!("Connected to server. Type a message and press Enter:");

    // One handle to write through, one (buffered) to read the reply through.
    let mut writer = stream.try_clone().expect("failed to clone stream");
    let mut reader = BufReader::new(stream);

    // Read lines from stdin and send them to the server.
    let stdin = io::stdin();
    for line in stdin.lock().lines() {
        let text = match line {
            Ok(t) => t,
            Err(_) => break,
        };

        if writeln!(writer, "{text}").is_err() {
            break;
        }

        // Read the server's response (terminated by '\n').
        let mut response = String::new();
        match reader.read_line(&mut response) {
            Ok(0) => break, // server closed the connection
            Ok(_) => print!("Server replied: {response}"),
            Err(e) => {
                eprintln!("Error reading from server: {e}");
                break;
            }
        }
    }
}
```

## Receiving One Character at a Time

The client above is designed for the echo server — it reads whole lines and sends messages. For our covert channel receiver, we need different behaviour:

- The client should **only receive** — it sends nothing to the server.
- It should **display each character as soon as it arrives**, rather than buffering until a newline or connection close.

Our overt message is ASCII, so we read **one byte at a time** and print it immediately. Bring the `Read` trait into scope for the single-byte `read`:

```rust
use std::io::Read;

// ...

let mut reader = BufReader::new(stream);
let mut byte = [0u8; 1];

loop {
    match reader.read(&mut byte) {
        // read() returning Ok(0) is the true end-of-stream: the server
        // closed the connection. (This is distinct from our "EOF" sentinel,
        // which arrives as ordinary bytes inside the timing pattern.)
        Ok(0) => {
            println!("\nServer closed connection.");
            break;
        }
        Ok(_) => {
            // Print the character immediately as it arrives, and flush so
            // it shows up right away rather than sitting in stdout's buffer.
            print!("{}", byte[0] as char);
            io::stdout().flush().ok();
        }
        Err(e) => {
            eprintln!("\nError reading from server: {e}");
            break;
        }
    }
}
```

## Measuring the Delays

We now need to measure the elapsed time between receiving successive characters and classify each gap as a `0` or `1`. Use `Instant::now()` before the read and `.elapsed()` after it to get the duration:

```rust
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

// ...

// Collect all measured durations for inspection.
let mut times: Vec<Duration> = Vec::new();

// ...

// Inside the receive loop, wrap the read:
let start = Instant::now();
let n = reader.read(&mut byte);
let elapsed = start.elapsed();

times.push(elapsed);
```

After the loop, print the collected durations to inspect them:

```rust
println!("{times:?}");
```

You should see two clusters of values — one near `ZERO` milliseconds and one near `ONE` milliseconds. This visual inspection step is useful for choosing a robust threshold before you write the classification logic.

## From Times to Characters {#sec-decode}

Once you can observe two distinct timing clusters, converting them to bits is straightforward: any duration above the midpoint threshold is a `1`, anything below is a `0`.

```rust
let threshold = Duration::from_millis((ZERO + ONE) / 2);
// threshold = 62 ms with our default constants

let mut covert_bits = String::new();
// For each measured `elapsed`:
if elapsed >= threshold {
    covert_bits.push('1');
} else {
    covert_bits.push('0');
}
```

Once you have accumulated enough bits, convert them back to characters. Process 8 bits at a time. A helper function in Rust might look like this:

```rust
fn bits_to_string(bits: &str) -> String {
    let mut result = String::new();
    let mut i = 0;

    // bits is a string of '0'/'1' (all ASCII), so byte offsets and char
    // offsets line up and slicing is safe.
    while i + 8 <= bits.len() {
        // Parse one byte (8 bits) as a base-2 integer.
        match u8::from_str_radix(&bits[i..i + 8], 2) {
            Ok(n) => result.push(n as char),
            Err(_) => result.push('?'), // bit error — character undecodable
        }
        i += 8;
    }
    result
}
```

Keep decoding until the recovered string ends with `"EOF"`, then strip the sentinel to reveal the covert message.

:::{.callout-note}
The entire **client** section of this lab has been intentionally vague — all the pieces are here but they are not assembled into a complete, working program. Code snippets are deliberately sparse. It is up to you to design a well-structured Rust program that:

1. Connects to the server
2. Receives the overt message one character at a time and prints it
3. Measures the inter-character delay for each received character
4. Classifies each delay as `0` or `1` using the midpoint threshold
5. Decodes the accumulated bit string into ASCII characters, 8 bits at a time
6. Stops when the `"EOF"` sentinel is detected
7. Prints the recovered covert message

*Good luck.*
:::
